prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms made it possible to measure time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B009 with Katori and Ye as my final position, unchanged from round 1. I reached it from a fifth-place opening ranking, and the chair is right that the committee should test that kind of movement rather than assume it. Having tested it against the full exchange, I still hold it, for three reasons. First, the invention is separable: a magic wavelength removes the lattice light shift, so many atoms can be interrogated without trap-induced perturbation, and that is what turns a neutral-atom clock into the most accurate measurement made in any field. Second, the confirmation is as firm as anything on the list: independent Sr and Yb realisations in several national laboratories, intercompared across continents. Third, the credit is as clean as this list allows, since all eight of us propose exactly Katori and Ye and nobody proposes a different or larger set. On the chair's question about delivered physics, the clearest items I can cite are routine clock comparisons at the 10^-18 level, which are themselves stringent tests of the stability of the transition frequencies, and resolution of the gravitational redshift across millimetre-scale height differences within a single lattice sample, as I recall it from Ye's group. I rely on recall for those details and have not verified them here. Dark-matter and constant-variation searches are still mostly prospective, and I would keep them out of the citation. As a theorist who has spent a career on spectra, I also value that the performance claims are credible because the relevant atomic structure, polarisabilities and blackbody shifts are understood well enough to be controlled.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one I voiced in round 1 and that the chair records: B009 sharpens an existing measurement rather than opening a new scientific question, whereas B018 opened a field and changed how we classify phases of matter. If the committee decides that the prize should reward a change in what physicists can think about rather than in what they can measure, B009 would drop in my ordering and I would want B018 discussed seriously. The second reservation is lineage: the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes cover neighbouring steps, and the citation must make clear that the lattice is a different idea. The third is credit: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat and the PTB and NIST groups made decisive accuracy demonstrations, and a two-name prize cannot recognise them. I treat these as real limits on how widely the citation can be phrased, not as reasons to reject the invention itself.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B009 first as measurement physics, credits Katori with the decisive magic-wavelength idea and Ye with the 1e-18 systematic frontier, discloses a research period in the Hall laboratory where Ye trained, and notes that the committee might prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and with how the disclosure was made. A research period in a laboratory where a candidate later trained is a historical professional tie and not a stake in the outcome, so I think recording it is sufficient and I would not ask Kroll to recuse. On waiting for the redefinition I disagree. The clocks are already the infrastructure on which that discussion rests, so the award does not depend on its outcome, and tying our decision to a metrological process we do not control would let an outside timetable replace a scientific judgement. For the same reason I would keep any mention of the redefinition out of the citation.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube to B009 but cautions that eight members ranking it should not be mistaken for depth of scientific weight, and notes that the clocks have not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of their own.
responses.response: I think that caution is right and I accept the second half of it: dark-matter couplings and variation of constants are prospective, and I have kept them out of my citation. I would draw the line on depth a little differently. Clock comparisons at the 10^-18 level and the redshift measurement within one lattice sample are precision tests that nature could have failed, but I will not oversell them as a discovery. We have both moved from lower or different openings, and I agree with the chair that this should be tested. For me the test is whether B009 survives the objection that it improves a measurement. I think it does on invention and confirmation, but not by so wide a margin that the committee should stop asking the question.

responses.point: Olsson keeps B009 as her preferred configuration with B017 (aberration-corrected electron optics, Rose, Haider, Urban) as a secondary alternative, and notes that lattice-clock history involves other groups and that Hall and Hansch were honoured in 2005 for comb technology.
responses.response: I agree that the two-name pairing simplifies the history and that Olsson's qualifications, other groups, the pending redefinition and the 2005 overlap, are real. I do not find them disqualifying, because the magic-wavelength idea is separable. On B017 I have not moved far from round 1. I would not object to it as a later prize, but the attribution gap is a point of substance for me: the corrector work on scanning instruments, which supplied much of the atomic-resolution spectroscopy I care about, lies outside Rose, Haider and Urban. That is why I carry B018 and B041 as my alternatives and not B017.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the B009 credit is unusually clean, that the 2005 and 2012 prizes concern different steps, and that the clock performance claims are trustworthy because relativistic atomic structure and blackbody and polarisability physics are understood.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and on the controlled atomic physics, which is the same reason I trust the 1e-18 claims. I would add one qualification to the claim that the 2005 and 2012 prizes concern different steps. They are different steps in one programme, so a reader will see a lineage, and the citation should say plainly that the lattice, not the comb or ion control, is what is recognised. On your question about Zoller in B014 and B010, it does not bear on my configuration, since I propose no second part. I would only note that combining the two would bring five distinct names, which exceeds the three-person limit, so the committee could not hold both together without cutting names.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B009 first on the argument that quantum projection noise falls with atom number, which is why lattice clocks surpass single-ion clocks, and notes that other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, the Yb and Hg communities) are not credited and that the dark-matter and geodesy payoffs are mostly projected.
responses.response: I accept the physical argument about atom number, and I think it is the cleanest explanation of why the lattice mattered more than a better version of an existing clock. I agree that the Yb and Hg communities and the Lemonde, Ludlow and Lisdat results go uncredited. My answer is that the citation should be written around the invention and its realization and around the magic-wavelength mechanism, with the 10^-18 level as an accomplishment and not as a record that can be overtaken. That is why my wording keeps both phrases and leaves out the redefinition and the prospective searches, on which your point about projected payoffs is correct.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats a precision-metrology invention as discovery-class, given the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I judge that it does, but I would revise if colleagues weight a change in what physicists can think about more heavily than I do.

Whether the citation can credit Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice and Ye for the accuracy and many-body frontier while making clear that other Sr, Yb and Hg groups, ion clocks and combs are not credited.
My account of delivered results, in particular the gravitational-redshift measurement within a single lattice sample, rests on recall and has not been verified against the record in front of me.

How B018 would compare if the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and of the three-dimensional topological-insulator work could be resolved. I regard the physics as strong but cannot settle the credit within the three supplied names.

Whether a computational-method prize such as B041 would be regarded as physics rather than chemistry, given the 1998 chemistry prize for density-functional theory. This affects only my second alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B009 is apparent from my profile: my field is electronic-structure theory, magnetism and spin dynamics, my doctorate was under Borje Johansson at Uppsala, and I worked at Los Alamos, none of which links me to Katori, Ye or their groups. I continue to disclose that my field is adjacent to B041 and B018, which is why I rank them only as alternatives and treat my earlier enthusiasm for B041 with caution. I also record my view that Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory tie calls for recording and not recusal.
